concepts.name: Definition and Nature of Commercialisation of Agriculture
key_dimensions: Distinction between subsistence farming and market-oriented farming
Whether commercialisation was voluntary (market-driven) or coercive (colonial compulsion) — UPSC trap: it was largely coercive, not a natural evolution
Role of railways, money economy, and market integration in enabling commercialisation
Difference between commercialisation in India vs. Western capitalist commercialisation

concepts.name: Revenue Settlements as a Driver of Commercialisation
key_dimensions: Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, and Mahalwari — how each forced cash-crop cultivation through cash-demand revenue
Why cash revenue demand compelled peasants to sell produce regardless of market conditions
Distinction: Permanent Settlement enriched zamindars but impoverished peasants; Ryotwari directly exposed peasant to state pressure
UPSC trap: Permanent Settlement is often linked only to land tenure, but its role in commercialisation is equally examinable

concepts.name: Indigo Cultivation and Plantation System
key_dimensions: Tinkathia system: forced cultivation of 3/20th of land with indigo — coercive nature
Indigo Revolt of 1859–60: causes, role of ryots, and significance as early agrarian resistance
Nil Darpan by Dinabandhu Mitra as a source for understanding planter exploitation
UPSC trap: Champaran Satyagraha (1917) targeted the same tinkathia system — linking colonial continuity

concepts.name: Cotton Cultivation and the American Civil War Effect
key_dimensions: How the American Civil War (1861–65) created a cotton boom in India — Berar and Deccan as key regions
Post-war collapse of cotton prices and its devastating effect on Deccan peasantry
Link between cotton boom, moneylender credit expansion, and subsequent debt trap
UPSC trap: The boom appeared as prosperity but structurally weakened peasant self-sufficiency

concepts.name: Opium Cultivation and State Monopoly
key_dimensions: East India Company's monopoly over opium production in Bengal and Bihar (Patna/Ghazipur)
Forced cultivation: peasants compelled to grow opium at below-market prices fixed by the Company
Opium as a key revenue source for British India and its role in the China trade triangle
UPSC trap: Opium is often examined under trade/revenue but is a classic case of coercive commercialisation

concepts.name: Jute Cultivation in Bengal
key_dimensions: Rise of jute as a cash crop in Bengal after 1850s driven by European demand
Paradox: Bengal grew raw jute but Dundee (Scotland) processed it — raw material export pattern
Swadeshi movement later attempted to develop indigenous jute mills as a counter
UPSC trap: Jute mills in Calcutta were mostly European-owned, not Indian — distinguishing ownership patterns

concepts.name: Wheat and Cash Crop Expansion in Punjab and United Provinces
key_dimensions: Canal colonisation in Punjab (especially after 1880s) and its role in wheat commercialisation
Link between railway expansion and wheat export from Punjab to world markets
How commercialisation in Punjab differed from Bengal — relatively more prosperous but also more market-vulnerable
Famine vulnerability: export of food grains even during scarcity — Digby's and Naoroji's critique

concepts.name: Role of Railways in Commercialisation of Agriculture
key_dimensions: Railways as 'drains' of raw materials to ports rather than integrating domestic markets
How railways helped British manufacturers penetrate Indian rural markets, destroying local industries
Positive colonial argument vs. nationalist critique — UPSC frequently tests both perspectives
UPSC trap: Railways aided commercialisation but did NOT lead to capitalist agricultural development — no reinvestment in land productivity

concepts.name: Moneylenders, Rural Indebtedness, and Commercialisation
key_dimensions: How cash-crop dependency increased peasant reliance on mahajans/sahukars for credit and seeds
Deccan Riots of 1875: direct link between moneylender exploitation and agrarian unrest
Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act (1879): colonial response — its limitations and significance
UPSC trap: Moneylenders are often seen as villains, but they also enabled commercialisation by providing credit — nuanced role

concepts.name: Decline of Food Crop Cultivation and Famine Linkage
key_dimensions: Shift from food crops to cash crops reduced food security at the village level
Famines of 1876–78 and 1896–97 — Romesh Chunder Dutt and Dadabhai Naoroji's argument linking commercialisation to famines
Famine Commission reports (1880, 1901) — official acknowledgment vs. nationalist interpretation
UPSC trap: British argued famines were due to drought; nationalists argued commercialisation and export policy were structural causes

concepts.name: Drain of Wealth Theory and Agricultural Commercialisation
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' — how agricultural surplus was drained via export of raw materials
R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' — systematic documentation of agricultural impoverishment
Difference between 'Home Charges' as financial drain and export of raw crops as material drain
UPSC trap: Drain theory is often linked only to finance — its agricultural dimension (raw material export without value addition) is equally important

concepts.name: Plantation Agriculture: Tea, Coffee, and Rubber
key_dimensions: Assam tea plantations — Indenture system (girmitiya labour), Workmen's Breach of Contract Act 1859 as instrument of labour bondage
Coffee plantations in Coorg and Nilgiris — similar enclave economy pattern
Plantations as 'enclaves': profits repatriated to Britain, no linkage with local Indian economy
UPSC trap: Plantation agriculture is commercialisation but NOT peasant commercialisation — it is settler/company-driven, a crucial distinction

concepts.name: Impact on Artisans and the Agrarian-Industrial Linkage
key_dimensions: De-industrialisation pushed artisans back to land, increasing pressure on agriculture
Over-crowding of agriculture: by 1901, over 70% of population dependent on agriculture — 'peasantisation' of artisans
How commercialisation of agriculture and de-industrialisation were two sides of the same colonial policy
UPSC trap: These are often taught separately but are structurally linked — integrated question likely

concepts.name: Land Alienation and Emergence of Absentee Landlordism
key_dimensions: How cash-crop debt cycles led to land mortgage and eventual transfer to moneylenders and merchants
Punjab Land Alienation Act 1900: colonial attempt to prevent land transfer to non-agriculturist classes — its motives (political stability) vs. economic impact
Rise of absentee landlords who had no interest in agricultural improvement
UPSC trap: Punjab Land Alienation Act is a rare example of British legislation protecting peasants — but motivated by fear of agrarian unrest, not welfare

concepts.name: Regional Variations in Commercialisation
key_dimensions: Bengal: jute and indigo; Punjab: wheat and cotton; Deccan: cotton; Assam: tea — each had distinct exploitative mechanisms
Why some regions (Punjab canal colonies) showed relative prosperity while others (Deccan, Bengal) showed acute distress
Role of geography, irrigation, and land tenure system in shaping regional outcomes
UPSC trap: Commercialisation is often generalised — questions may test regional specificity

concepts.name: Agrarian Legislation and Its Inadequacy
key_dimensions: Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act 1879, Punjab Land Alienation Act 1900, Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 — purpose and limitations
Why colonial agrarian legislation was reactive (responding to unrest) rather than proactive
Tenancy rights vs. occupancy rights distinction in Bengal Tenancy Act — UPSC favourite trap
Contrast with post-independence land reforms — what colonial legislation deliberately avoided (redistribution)

concepts.name: Nationalist Critique of Commercialisation: Economic Nationalist School
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji, R.C. Dutt, G.K. Gokhale — their specific arguments regarding agricultural exploitation
How the economic nationalist critique formed the intellectual foundation of the independence movement
Cambridge School counter-argument: commercialisation as modernisation — UPSC tests ability to evaluate historiographical debates
UPSC trap: Distinguish between Early Nationalists' economic critique and the later Gandhian critique of industrialism itself

concepts.name: Commercialisation and the Changing Agrarian Class Structure
key_dimensions: Emergence of new classes: rich peasants/kulaks, landless labourers, moneylender-merchants
Decline of village self-sufficiency (jajmani system) due to market penetration
How commercialisation created conditions for later peasant movements (Kisan Sabhas, Non-Cooperation)
UPSC trap: Class differentiation in rural India is often linked to post-independence politics but its roots lie in colonial commercialisation

concepts.name: Export Statistics and the Paradox of Agricultural Commercialisation
key_dimensions: India became a major exporter of raw materials (cotton, jute, opium, wheat, indigo) while importing finished goods — classic colonial trade pattern
R.C. Dutt's data: export surplus did not benefit Indian farmers but was extracted as 'Home Charges'
Paradox: high export volumes coexisted with peasant poverty and recurring famines
UPSC trap: Export growth is NOT evidence of agricultural prosperity — the distribution of benefits is the key analytical lens
